meta.title: Deep Time — A Timeline of Earth and Life
meta.description: Geological time scale plus major events from the formation of Earth to the present day.

units.ybp: Years before the reference year. All time math should use this field.
units.ma: Millions of years ago. Convenience field; equals ybp / 1000000.
units.year: Calendar year (negative = BCE). Only present for events with a known calendar date.

certaintyLevels.firm: Well-constrained; dated directly and widely agreed.
certaintyLevels.approximate: Good consensus on the ballpark, but the exact figure shifts with new finds.
certaintyLevels.debated: Actively argued over. Treat as one plausible estimate, not a fact.

categories.origin: First appearance of a group of living things
categories.climate: Ice ages, warming events, atmospheric change
categories.geology: Continents, oceans, and the planet itself

sources: International Commission on Stratigraphy, International Chronostratigraphic Chart (v2023/09)
Peer-reviewed consensus dates for individual first-appearance and extinction events
meta.caveat: Deep dates carry real uncertainty — often tens of millions of years for early life. Every entry carries a certainty field; respect it rather than presenting these as exact.

scale.name: Hadean
scale.blurb: A molten, hellish world under constant bombardment. Named for Hades.

scale.name: Archean
scale.blurb: Oceans form, the first life appears, and the sky has no oxygen.

scale.name: Proterozoic
scale.blurb: Oxygen floods the air, complex cells evolve, and the planet freezes over twice.

scale.name: Phanerozoic
scale.blurb: The age of visible life — everything with shells, bones, leaves, and legs.

scale.name: Paleozoic
scale.blurb: Life conquers the sea, then the land. Ends in the worst catastrophe ever.

scale.name: Mesozoic
scale.blurb: The age of dinosaurs, from the Great Dying to the asteroid.

scale.name: Cenozoic
scale.blurb: The age of mammals, grass, and eventually us.

scale.name: Cryogenian
scale.blurb: Snowball Earth — glaciers reach the equator, twice.

scale.name: Ediacaran
scale.blurb: The first large, soft-bodied animals — unlike anything alive today.

scale.name: Cambrian
scale.blurb: Almost every animal body plan appears in a geological instant.

scale.name: Ordovician
scale.blurb: Sea life diversifies wildly; the first plants creep onto land.

scale.name: Silurian
scale.blurb: Jawed fish, and the first animals to walk on dry land.

scale.name: Devonian
scale.blurb: The Age of Fishes. Forests appear, and fins become feet.

scale.name: Carboniferous
scale.blurb: Vast coal swamps, 35% oxygen, and dragonflies the size of hawks.

scale.name: Permian
scale.blurb: One giant continent, sprawling deserts, and the rise of reptiles.

scale.name: Triassic
scale.blurb: Recovery from the Great Dying. The first dinosaurs and first mammals.

scale.name: Jurassic
scale.blurb: Giant sauropods, the first birds, and Pangaea tearing apart.

scale.name: Cretaceous
scale.blurb: Flowers bloom, T. rex hunts, and it ends with a bang.

scale.name: Paleogene
scale.blurb: Mammals inherit an empty world and get big fast.

scale.name: Neogene
scale.blurb: Grasslands spread, apes diversify, and our lineage splits off.

scale.name: Quaternary
scale.blurb: Repeating ice ages — and the whole human story.

scale.name: Pleistocene
scale.blurb: The Ice Age proper — mammoths, cave lions, and glaciers to Ohio.

scale.name: Holocene
scale.blurb: The warm window in which every civilization has existed.

events.label: The Sun ignites
events.blurb: A collapsing cloud of gas and dust lights up as a star. The leftover debris disk becomes the planets, including ours.

events.label: Earth forms
events.blurb: Dust and rock in the young Sun's disk clump together into a planet in perhaps 10-20 million years.

events.label: A Mars-sized world hits Earth; the Moon forms
events.blurb: The impactor, nicknamed Theia, blasts enough debris into orbit to coalesce into the Moon. Earth's day is about 5 hours long afterward.

events.label: Liquid water oceans appear
events.blurb: Zircon crystals from Australia hint that Earth had cooled enough for oceans surprisingly early.

events.label: Late Heavy Bombardment
events.blurb: A proposed storm of asteroids batters the inner planets — the source of most large lunar craters. Whether it was a distinct spike is still argued.

events.label: Oldest surviving rocks
events.blurb: The Acasta Gneiss in Canada is the oldest intact rock we can still put our hands on. Everything older has been recycled by the planet.

events.label: Life begins
events.blurb: Chemical signatures in ancient rocks suggest single-celled life already existed. Everything alive today descends from one of these populations.

events.label: Bacteria and Archaea split
events.blurb: Life's deepest fork. Archaea look like bacteria but are biochemically alien — and one of them eventually became the ancestor of you.

events.label: Oldest clear microbial fossils
events.blurb: Layered mats of bacteria — stromatolites — leave unmistakable structures in Australian rock. Living versions still grow in Shark Bay.

events.label: Photosynthesis evolves
events.blurb: Early microbes learn to run on sunlight. The first versions produce no oxygen at all.

events.label: Plate tectonics begins
events.blurb: Earth's crust breaks into drifting plates — the engine behind every mountain range, earthquake, and ocean. When it started is genuinely contested.

events.label: Cyanobacteria start making oxygen
events.blurb: A new kind of photosynthesis splits water and dumps oxygen as waste. It will remake the entire planet.

events.label: Great Oxidation Event
events.blurb: Oxygen finally builds up in the air. To most life at the time it is a deadly poison — probably the largest extinction in Earth's history, and it left no fossils.

events.label: Huronian glaciation — first great ice age
events.blurb: Rising oxygen destroys atmospheric methane, and the planet plunges into a 300-million-year freeze.

events.label: Vredefort impact — the largest known crater
events.blurb: An asteroid perhaps 20 km across leaves a scar over 300 km wide in what is now South Africa. Life at the time was still entirely single-celled.

events.label: Complex cells (eukaryotes) evolve
events.blurb: One cell swallows another and keeps it. That captive becomes the mitochondrion — the power plant in every cell of your body.

events.label: The Boring Billion
events.blurb: A billion years of remarkably little change: stable climate, stable chemistry, almost no evolutionary drama. Life spent it quietly getting ready.

events.label: Plants capture chloroplasts
events.blurb: A cell swallows a cyanobacterium and keeps it as a solar panel. Every leaf, blade of grass, and alga runs on that captive to this day.

events.label: Sexual reproduction appears
events.blurb: Shuffling genes between two parents massively speeds up evolution. Fossil red algae show the earliest good evidence.

events.label: Rodinia, an earlier supercontinent
events.blurb: Long before Pangaea, the continents gathered into Rodinia. Its breakup may have helped trigger Snowball Earth.

events.label: First multicellular life
events.blurb: Bangiomorpha, a fossil red seaweed, is the oldest known organism made of specialized cells working as one body.

events.label: First fungi
events.blurb: Fungi are closer relatives of animals than of plants. Later they become the partner that lets plants colonise land at all.

events.label: Snowball Earth
events.blurb: Two enormous glaciations — the Sturtian and Marinoan — may have carried ice sheets all the way to the equator.

events.label: First animals (sponges)
events.blurb: Molecular clocks put the animal kingdom's origin here, though convincing sponge fossils come later. Every animal, including you, traces back to this branch.

events.label: Ediacaran biota — the strange first big life
events.blurb: Fronds, discs, and quilted bags up to a meter across. Many are so alien that scientists still argue whether they were animals at all.

events.label: Cambrian Explosion
events.blurb: In roughly 25 million years, nearly every major animal body plan alive today shows up — along with eyes, shells, guts, and predators.

events.label: First vertebrates — jawless fish
events.blurb: Small, finless swimmers like Haikouichthys have the first true backbones. This is the start of our own lineage.

events.label: Trilobites appear
events.blurb: The signature fossil of the Paleozoic. They survive for 270 million years — longer than dinosaurs — in over 20,000 species.

events.label: The first great predators
events.blurb: Anomalocaris, a metre-long hunter with grasping arms and compound eyes, sits atop the Cambrian food chain. Being eaten becomes an evolutionary force.

events.label: Plants move onto land
events.blurb: Mossy, rootless pioneers colonize bare rock, beginning the long process of building soil.

events.label: Ordovician-Silurian extinction
events.blurb: The second-deadliest mass extinction: about 85% of species vanish as a sudden glaciation drops sea levels worldwide.

events.label: Animals crawl onto land
events.blurb: Millipede-like arthropods are the first animals to live out of water — 60 million years before anything with a backbone follows.

events.label: Fish evolve jaws
events.blurb: Hinged jaws turn fish from filter-feeders into hunters. Your own jaw is a direct descendant of this innovation.

events.label: Sharks appear
events.blurb: Sharks are older than trees, older than Saturn's rings, and have outlasted all five mass extinctions since.

events.label: First insects
events.blurb: Six legs, three body segments. Insects will go on to become the most species-rich group of animals on Earth.

events.label: First forests
events.blurb: Archaeopteris grows 30 meters tall with real wood and roots. Deep roots crack rock and pull CO2 from the air, cooling the planet.

events.label: Fins become legs — first tetrapods
events.blurb: Fish like Tiktaalik have shoulders, elbows, wrists, and a neck. Every amphibian, reptile, bird, and mammal is a modified fish because of this.

events.label: Late Devonian extinction
events.blurb: A drawn-out series of pulses wipes out roughly 75% of species, hitting reef ecosystems especially hard.

events.label: Seeds evolve
events.blurb: A packaged embryo with its own lunchbox. Seeds let plants finally spread into dry ground far from water.

events.label: Coal swamps and giant insects
events.blurb: Oxygen peaks near 35% of the atmosphere, letting dragonflies reach 70 cm wingspans. Buried swamp plants become nearly all the coal we burn today.

events.label: First reptiles
events.blurb: The shelled egg frees vertebrates from water entirely. Hylonomus, a lizard-like animal about 20 cm long, is among the earliest known.

events.label: Carboniferous rainforest collapse
events.blurb: The great coal forests fragment and die as the climate dries. Amphibians crash; reptiles, freed from needing water, take over.

events.label: Pangaea fully assembled
events.blurb: Nearly all land on Earth is welded into one supercontinent, surrounded by a single global ocean. You could walk from the South Pole to the Arctic.

events.label: Capitanian extinction
events.blurb: A serious extinction only recognised recently, striking eight million years before the Great Dying finished the job.

events.label: Siberian Traps erupt
events.blurb: Lava floods an area the size of Europe for a million years, belching CO2 and sulphur. This is the murder weapon behind the Great Dying.

events.label: The Great Dying
events.blurb: The worst extinction ever: up to 90% of marine species die as Siberian volcanoes erupt for a million years, acidifying and cooking the oceans. Life takes 10 million years to recover.

events.label: Trilobites vanish
events.blurb: After 270 million years and tens of thousands of species, trilobites are wiped out completely in the Great Dying.

events.label: Reptiles return to the sea
events.blurb: Ichthyosaurs re-enter the ocean and converge on a dolphin shape. Some give birth to live young, tail-first, underwater.

events.label: First dinosaurs
events.blurb: The earliest unambiguous dinosaurs are small, fast bipeds a couple of meters long — nothing like the giants to come.

events.label: First turtles
events.blurb: The shell is a rebuilt ribcage — an anatomy so odd that its origin puzzled biologists for a century.

events.label: Pterosaurs take flight
events.blurb: The first vertebrates to truly fly, tens of millions of years before birds. The largest had the wingspan of a small aircraft.

events.label: First mammals
events.blurb: Shrew-sized, furry, warm-blooded, and probably nocturnal. Mammals spend their first 160 million years staying small and out of the way.

events.label: Triassic-Jurassic extinction
events.blurb: Massive volcanism as Pangaea begins to rift kills off about 75% of species — and clears the field for dinosaurs to dominate.

events.label: First crocodilians
events.blurb: Crocodiles arrive before the first birds and change remarkably little afterwards. They watched the dinosaurs come and go.

events.label: First frogs
events.blurb: Frogs work out the jump-and-croak formula early and stick with it through two mass extinctions.

events.label: Pangaea breaks apart
events.blurb: The supercontinent splits, opening the Atlantic. Isolated landmasses send life down separate evolutionary paths.

events.label: Giant sauropods roam
events.blurb: Brachiosaurus and kin become the largest land animals ever — some over 30 meters long and 50 tonnes.

events.label: Stegosaurus
events.blurb: Plates along the back, spikes on the tail, and a brain the size of a lime. It died out 80 million years before T. rex appeared.

events.label: First birds
events.blurb: Archaeopteryx has feathers and wings but also teeth and a long bony tail. Birds are dinosaurs — the only lineage that survived.

events.label: Ants and the social insects
events.blurb: Colonies behave like a single organism. Today ants alone weigh roughly as much as all wild birds and mammals combined.

events.label: Flowering plants appear
events.blurb: Flowers strike a deal with insects: pollen delivery in exchange for nectar. Angiosperms now make up about 90% of all plant species.

events.label: First snakes
events.blurb: Lizards that gave up their legs. Some snakes still carry tiny vestigial hip bones as a souvenir.

events.label: Pouched mammals split off
events.blurb: Marsupials give birth to tiny, half-formed young that finish developing in a pouch — a different bet from the placental one.

events.label: Bees evolve alongside flowers
events.blurb: Wasps go vegetarian and start trading pollination for nectar. Flowering plants explode in diversity as a result.

events.label: Peak Cretaceous hothouse
events.blurb: No ice anywhere on Earth. Forests grow inside the Antarctic Circle and shallow seas split continents in half.

events.label: Mosasaurs rule the seas
events.blurb: Giant marine lizards, closer kin to monitor lizards and snakes than to dinosaurs. They died with the dinosaurs at the same instant.

events.label: Velociraptor
events.blurb: The real animal was turkey-sized and covered in feathers — a long way from the scaly film version.

events.label: Tyrannosaurus rex
events.blurb: T. rex lives only in the final 2 million years of the dinosaur age — closer in time to us than to Stegosaurus, which died out 80 million years earlier.

events.label: Triceratops
events.blurb: Three horns and one of the largest skulls of any land animal ever. It lived alongside T. rex right up to the final day.

events.label: Deccan Traps erupt
events.blurb: Enormous volcanism in India brackets the asteroid impact. Scientists still argue how much of the dinosaur extinction each one caused.

events.label: Asteroid strikes; dinosaurs die
events.blurb: A 10 km asteroid hits the Yucatan at Chicxulub. About 75% of species die, including every dinosaur except birds. Mammals inherit the planet.

events.label: First primates
events.blurb: Small, tree-dwelling insect-eaters with grasping hands and forward-facing eyes appear almost immediately after the asteroid.

events.label: Placental mammals radiate
events.blurb: With the dinosaurs gone, placental mammals explode into every vacant role in a few million years. Most mammals alive today are on this branch.

events.label: Terror birds
events.blurb: Flightless predatory birds up to three metres tall, with axe-shaped beaks. For millions of years South America's top predator was a bird.

events.label: First elephant relatives
events.blurb: The earliest proboscideans are pig-sized and tuskless. The trunk and tusks come much later.

events.label: First penguins
events.blurb: Penguins give up flight almost immediately after the asteroid. Some early species stood as tall as a person.

events.label: Titanoboa, the largest snake ever
events.blurb: Thirteen metres long and over a tonne. It could only exist because the tropics after the asteroid were so persistently hot.

events.label: Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum
events.blurb: A colossal carbon release warms the planet 5-8°C in a few thousand years. Crocodiles live in the Arctic. It is the closest natural analogue to modern warming.

events.label: First horses
events.blurb: Eohippus is the size of a small dog with four toes on each front foot. The horse lineage is one of the best-documented in all of palaeontology.

events.label: Grasses appear
events.blurb: Grass grows from the base, not the tip, so it survives being eaten and burned. That one trick eventually reshapes whole continents.

events.label: Early Eocene Climatic Optimum
events.blurb: The warmest sustained stretch of the last 66 million years. Palms grow in Alaska and the poles are ice-free.

events.label: Bats take flight
events.blurb: The only mammals with powered flight. Fossils show flight evolved before echolocation, not the other way round.

events.label: Whales return to the sea
events.blurb: Hoofed land mammals related to hippos go back into the water. Fossils track the whole transition — Pakicetus walked, Basilosaurus swam.

events.label: India hits Asia; the Himalayas rise
events.blurb: India slams north after a 6,000 km solo voyage. The collision is still happening, and Everest still grows a few millimetres a year.

events.label: The Azolla event
events.blurb: A freshwater fern may have blanketed the Arctic Ocean and drawn down so much CO2 that it helped tip Earth into the current icehouse.

events.label: New and Old World monkeys split
events.blurb: Monkeys reach South America, most likely rafting across a narrower Atlantic on floating vegetation.

events.label: First dogs and wolves
events.blurb: The dog family emerges in North America and eventually spreads worldwide — the ancestors of every wolf, fox, and household dog.

events.label: Antarctica freezes over
events.blurb: As Antarctica isolates and CO2 falls, permanent ice sheets form. Earth shifts from a hothouse to the icehouse world we still live in.

events.label: Grasslands spread worldwide
events.blurb: Grasses take over drying continents, driving the evolution of grazers with high-crowned teeth — horses, antelope, cattle.

events.label: Eocene-Oligocene extinction
events.blurb: Called the Grande Coupure — the great cut. As Antarctica freezes, tropical forests retreat and their inhabitants go with them.

events.label: First cats
events.blurb: The cat family appears and changes very little afterwards — the basic ambush-predator design was right the first time.

events.label: Megalodon
events.blurb: A shark up to 18 metres long with teeth the size of a hand. It hunted whales and vanished as the oceans cooled.

events.label: Gibbons split off
events.blurb: The lesser apes take to swinging beneath branches, and evolve arms long enough to make it look effortless.

events.label: Great apes diverge
events.blurb: Orangutans split from the line leading to gorillas, chimps, and humans. Big-bodied, big-brained, slow-breeding apes spread across Africa and Asia.

events.label: Human and chimpanzee lines split
events.blurb: Our last common ancestor with chimpanzees lives around here. Neither species existed yet — both descend from it.

events.label: The Grand Canyon is carved
events.blurb: The Colorado River cuts down through two billion years of rock — a cross-section of nearly half of Earth's history in one gorge.

events.label: The Mediterranean dries up
events.blurb: Cut off from the Atlantic, the entire Mediterranean evaporates into a deep salt desert, kilometres below sea level.

events.label: The Zanclean flood refills it
events.blurb: The Atlantic breaks back through Gibraltar and refills the Mediterranean, possibly in as little as a couple of years. Likely the largest flood in Earth's history.

events.label: Upright walking
events.blurb: Australopithecus walks fully upright — the Laetoli footprints show a modern human stride 3.7 million years ago. Big brains come much later.

events.label: First stone tools
events.blurb: Sharp flakes from Lomekwi, Kenya, predate our own genus. Somebody in our family tree was making cutting edges before Homo existed.

events.label: Lucy walks in Ethiopia
events.blurb: Forty percent of one Australopithecus skeleton, showing beyond doubt that our ancestors walked upright while still having ape-sized brains.

events.label: Genus Homo appears
events.blurb: Smaller faces, bigger brains, and a committed reliance on tools and meat. The earliest fossils assigned to our genus are frustratingly fragmentary.

events.label: The Isthmus of Panama closes
events.blurb: North and South America join. Animals swap continents, Atlantic and Pacific waters are separated, and global ocean currents reorganise.

events.label: The Ice Ages begin
events.blurb: Not one ice age but dozens, cycling roughly every 100,000 years as Earth's orbit wobbles. Ice sheets repeatedly bury Canada and northern Europe.

events.label: Sabertooth cats
events.blurb: Smilodon's canines reached 28 cm. It survived until the end of the last ice age and overlapped with people for thousands of years.

events.label: Homo habilis
events.blurb: The 'handy man' — small-brained by our standards but a consistent toolmaker, and long treated as the first true member of our genus.

events.label: Homo erectus — the first great traveler
events.blurb: Body proportions much like ours, and the first hominin to leave Africa — reaching China and Indonesia. It survives nearly 2 million years, ten times longer than us so far.

events.label: The hand axe — the first standard design
events.blurb: A teardrop-shaped tool made to the same template across Africa, Europe, and Asia for over a million years. The longest-running design in human history.

events.label: Mid-Pleistocene Transition
events.blurb: The ice-age rhythm shifts from a 41,000-year beat to a 100,000-year one, with deeper, longer glaciations. Why is still unresolved.

events.label: Control of fire
events.blurb: Hearths appear in the archaeological record. Cooking unlocks far more calories from food and may have paid for our expensive brains.

events.label: Neanderthals
events.blurb: Cold-adapted, big-brained, and skilled toolmakers who buried their dead. They interbred with us — most people outside Africa carry 1-2% Neanderthal DNA.

events.label: Woolly mammoths
events.blurb: The last mammoths were still alive on Wrangel Island in the Arctic while the Egyptians were building pyramids.

events.label: Denisovans
events.blurb: An entire human species identified mainly from DNA in a finger bone. Their genes survive in people across Asia and the Pacific today.

events.label: Homo sapiens appears
events.blurb: Anatomically modern humans emerge in Africa. Fossils from Jebel Irhoud, Morocco, push our origin far earlier than once thought.

events.label: Mitochondrial Eve
events.blurb: The woman from whom every living person inherits their mitochondrial DNA. She was not the only woman alive — just the one whose line never broke.

events.label: Symbols and ornament appear
events.blurb: Deliberate ochre engravings and pierced shell beads at Blombos Cave in South Africa — the earliest firm evidence of minds that deal in symbols.

events.label: Homo floresiensis, the 'hobbit'
events.blurb: A metre-tall human species isolated on the Indonesian island of Flores, living alongside dwarf elephants and giant rats.

events.label: Toba supervolcano erupts
events.blurb: The largest eruption in two million years blankets South Asia in ash and may have cooled the planet for years.

events.label: A possible human bottleneck
events.blurb: One reading of our genetics suggests humanity crashed to a few thousand individuals around the Toba eruption. The evidence is heavily disputed.

events.label: Out of Africa
events.blurb: The migration that populated the world. Every non-African alive today descends largely from this relatively small group.

events.label: People reach Australia
events.blurb: Crossing open ocean to Sahul requires real boats — the earliest strong evidence of deliberate sea voyaging.

events.label: The bow and arrow
events.blurb: Stone points from Sibudu, South Africa, look like arrowheads. Killing at a distance changes hunting and, eventually, warfare.

events.label: Megafauna extinction
events.blurb: Mammoths, giant sloths, sabertooths, and moa disappear continent by continent, closely tracking the arrival of humans. Climate change and hunting both played a part.

events.label: Cave art
events.blurb: A warty pig painted on a wall in Sulawesi is the oldest known figurative art. Chauvet and Lascaux follow thousands of years later.

events.label: Oldest musical instruments
events.blurb: Flutes carved from bird bone and mammoth ivory, found in German caves. They play a recognisable scale.

events.label: Last Glacial Maximum
events.blurb: Ice sheets reach their peak. Sea level sits about 125 m lower, exposing land bridges — including the one from Siberia to Alaska.

events.label: Dogs domesticated
events.blurb: Wolves become companions — the first domesticated animal, thousands of years before any crop or livestock.

events.label: Pottery invented
events.blurb: Fired clay pots appear in China during the ice age — thousands of years before farming, made by hunter-gatherers.

events.label: People reach the Americas
events.blurb: Migration from Siberia into a continent with no humans in it. Some sites, like White Sands footprints, may push this back to 23,000 years.

events.label: Fermentation and beer
events.blurb: Residues in stone vessels in Israel suggest brewing predates bread and farming. Some archaeologists think beer helped motivate agriculture.

events.label: Younger Dryas cold snap
events.blurb: The warming world lurches back into near-glacial cold within decades, then recovers just as abruptly. Proof that climate can flip fast.

events.label: Agriculture invented
events.blurb: Farming begins independently in at least 11 regions — wheat in the Fertile Crescent, rice in China, maize in Mexico, potatoes in the Andes. Everything else follows from this.

events.label: Holocene begins — the warm window
events.blurb: The current interglacial starts. Every city, empire, and written word in human history fits inside it.

events.label: Göbekli Tepe
events.blurb: Massive carved stone pillars raised by hunter-gatherers — before pottery, metal, writing, or farming. It overturned the assumption that farming had to come first.

events.label: First walled towns
events.blurb: Jericho and Çatalhöyük hold thousands of people — permanent settlement on a scale never seen before.

events.label: The Green Sahara
events.blurb: The Sahara is grassland and lakes, full of hippos, crocodiles, and cattle herders. Rock art there still shows people swimming.

events.label: Cats domesticate themselves
events.blurb: Grain stores drew mice, and mice drew wildcats. A cat was buried with a human on Cyprus 9,500 years ago.

events.label: Doggerland drowns
events.blurb: The rich lowland connecting Britain to Europe is swallowed by rising seas. Trawlers still dredge up its mammoth bones and stone tools.

events.label: The 8.2 kiloyear cooling event
events.blurb: A glacial lake bursts into the North Atlantic and shuts down ocean circulation. The northern hemisphere cools sharply for about 150 years.

events.label: Lactose tolerance spreads
events.blurb: A mutation lets adults digest milk. It sweeps through herding populations — one of the fastest known cases of recent human evolution.

events.label: The wheel
events.blurb: First used for pottery, then carts. Notably, it was never adopted for transport in the pre-Columbian Americas — there were no draft animals to pull it.

events.label: Horses domesticated
events.blurb: On the steppe, horses become transport. Speed reshapes trade, migration, and warfare for the next 5,000 years.

events.label: Uruk, the first city
events.blurb: Tens of thousands of people living together in Mesopotamia, requiring the invention of administration, accounting, and eventually writing.

events.label: Bronze Age
events.blurb: Alloying copper with tin makes the first hard metal tools, and the first long-distance trade networks to supply them.

events.label: Writing invented
events.blurb: Sumerian cuneiform starts as accounting marks on clay. History, in the literal sense of written record, begins here.

events.label: Stonehenge raised
events.blurb: Built in stages over 1,500 years, aligned to the solstices, with some stones hauled 250 km from Wales.

events.label: The Indus Valley civilization
events.blurb: Gridded streets, standardised bricks, and covered drains across a vast area — with no clear palaces or royal tombs. Its script remains undeciphered.

events.label: Great Pyramid of Giza built
events.blurb: It stayed the tallest structure humans had ever built for about 3,800 years. Cleopatra lived closer to us in time than to its construction.

events.label: The 4.2 kiloyear drought
events.blurb: A severe, widespread drought coincides with the collapse of the Akkadian Empire and upheaval in Egypt and the Indus Valley.

events.label: The Code of Hammurabi
events.blurb: Laws carved on a public stone pillar so that everyone could see them. The idea that rules should be written down and fixed in advance starts here.

events.label: Chickens domesticated
events.blurb: Red junglefowl in Southeast Asia become chickens, probably drawn in by rice farming. There are now about 26 billion of them — the most numerous bird on Earth, and the closest living relative you can eat to a tyrannosaur.

events.label: The Bronze Age Collapse
events.blurb: Within decades, nearly every eastern Mediterranean civilization falls. Cities burn, trade networks vanish, and writing is lost in Greece for 400 years.

events.label: Iron Age
events.blurb: Iron is far more common than tin, so good tools and weapons stop being a luxury of the elite.

events.label: The alphabet
events.blurb: Phoenician traders reduce writing to about 22 signs for sounds. Literacy stops being a specialist profession.

events.label: Polynesians settle the Pacific
events.blurb: Voyagers cross thousands of kilometres of open ocean by stars, swell, and birds, finding specks of land in the largest empty space on Earth.

events.label: Classical Greece, Persia, and the Warring States
events.blurb: A remarkable few centuries: Athenian democracy, Greek philosophy, the Achaemenid Empire, Confucius, the Buddha, and the first Chinese unification all fall close together.

events.label: China unified; the Great Wall begun
events.blurb: Qin Shi Huang standardises script, weights, currency, and even axle widths — and is buried with an army of 8,000 terracotta soldiers.

events.label: The Silk Road opens
events.blurb: Regular trade links China to the Mediterranean. Silk, paper, and gunpowder travel west; so, later, does the Black Death.

events.label: Roman Empire
events.blurb: From Augustus to the fall of the West in 476 CE. At its height it governed roughly a quarter of humanity.

events.label: Paper invented
events.blurb: Cai Lun refines papermaking in Han China. Cheap writing material spreads west over the next thousand years and eventually makes printing worthwhile.

events.label: The Maya Classic period
events.blurb: Mesoamerican city-states with full writing, a place-value number system including zero, and astronomy accurate to minutes per century.

events.label: Zero becomes a number
events.blurb: Brahmagupta writes rules for calculating with zero and negative numbers. Modern mathematics, and every computer, rests on this.

events.label: Islamic Golden Age
events.blurb: Baghdad, Córdoba, and Cairo lead the world in mathematics, astronomy, medicine, and optics. Algebra and our numerals come through this era.

events.label: Gunpowder
events.blurb: Chinese alchemists looking for an elixir of immortality find an explosive instead. It ends the era of castle walls.

events.label: Medieval Warm Period
events.blurb: A warm spell in the North Atlantic. Norse farmers settle Greenland — and abandon it when the warmth fades.

events.label: The magnetic compass
events.blurb: Navigation stops depending on clear skies and a visible coastline. Open-ocean voyaging becomes practical.

events.label: Angkor Wat built
events.blurb: The largest religious structure ever built, at the heart of a city of perhaps 750,000 people — the largest in the pre-industrial world.

events.label: The Mongol Empire
events.blurb: The largest contiguous land empire in history, assembled in a single lifetime and held together by horses and an early postal relay system.

events.label: The Little Ice Age
events.blurb: Alpine glaciers advance over villages and the Thames freezes hard enough to hold fairs on the ice.

events.label: The Black Death
events.blurb: Plague kills perhaps half of Europe in six years. The resulting labour shortage raises wages and helps unravel serfdom.

events.label: The Renaissance
events.blurb: Rediscovered classical learning, linear perspective, anatomy, and a new confidence that the world could be measured and depicted accurately.

events.label: The Aztec and Inca empires
events.blurb: Millions of people, vast road networks, and cities larger than any in Europe — brought down within years by steel, horses, and above all smallpox.

events.label: Printing press
events.blurb: Gutenberg's movable type makes books cheap in Europe. Movable type existed in China centuries earlier, but Europe's alphabet suited it better.

events.label: Columbian Exchange begins
events.blurb: Two biological worlds separated for 12,000 years collide. Crops, animals, and — devastatingly — diseases move both ways, killing perhaps 90% of the Americas' population.

events.label: The world sailed round
events.blurb: Magellan's expedition returns with 18 of its original 270 men. The Earth is confirmed, in practice, to be a globe you can go all the way around.

events.label: Scientific Revolution
events.blurb: Copernicus to Newton. Explaining nature by testable mathematical law rather than authority turns out to be the most productive idea humans have ever had.

events.label: The telescope
events.blurb: Within two years Galileo sees moons orbiting Jupiter — plain evidence that not everything goes around the Earth.

events.label: The dodo goes extinct
events.blurb: Flightless and unafraid of people, the dodo lasts under a century after sailors reach Mauritius. It becomes the emblem of human-caused extinction.

events.label: Newton's Principia
events.blurb: One set of equations governs both a falling apple and an orbiting moon. The idea that the universe follows universal, discoverable law is established.

events.label: Industrial Revolution
events.blurb: Coal-fired steam power ends the age of muscle and water. Human population and atmospheric CO2 both start climbing steeply from here.

events.label: The American and French Revolutions
events.blurb: Government by consent rather than birth moves from philosophy to practice, and the idea proves impossible to contain.

events.label: Deep time discovered
events.blurb: James Hutton looks at Siccar Point and realizes Earth is unimaginably older than a few thousand years. Everything on this timeline before written history is a consequence of that insight.

events.label: The first vaccine
events.blurb: Edward Jenner uses cowpox to protect against smallpox — the first deliberate immunisation, and eventually the tool that eradicates the disease entirely.

events.label: One billion humans
events.blurb: It took all of human history to reach the first billion. The eighth arrived in about twelve years.

events.label: Tambora and the year without a summer
events.blurb: The largest eruption in recorded history causes crop failures worldwide. Snow falls in New England in June, and a rainy Swiss holiday produces Frankenstein.

events.label: Photography
events.blurb: For the first time, a moment can be recorded exactly rather than remembered or drawn.

events.label: Abolition of slavery
events.blurb: From the British Empire in 1833 to Brazil in 1888, legal slavery is dismantled across the Atlantic world after millennia as a near-universal institution.

events.label: The telegraph
events.blurb: Messages outrun horses and ships for the first time in history. Distance stops being the same thing as delay.

events.label: Anaesthesia
events.blurb: Surgery stops being torture. Operations can finally take as long as they need to.

events.label: On the Origin of Species published
events.blurb: Darwin explains how the whole branching tree on this timeline came to be, without needing a designer.

events.label: Germ theory and vaccines
events.blurb: Pasteur and Koch show that microbes cause disease. Average human life expectancy roughly doubles over the following century.

events.label: The periodic table
events.blurb: Mendeleev arranges the elements by their properties and leaves gaps — then the missing elements are found, exactly as predicted.

events.label: The telephone
events.blurb: The human voice travels down a wire. Real-time conversation across distance becomes ordinary.

events.label: Electric light and the power grid
events.blurb: Cheap indoor light detaches human activity from the sun, restructuring work, cities, and sleep itself.

events.label: X-rays
events.blurb: Röntgen photographs the bones of his wife's hand. Medicine can see inside a living body without opening it.

events.label: Radio
events.blurb: Information travels without any wire at all — the beginning of broadcasting, and eventually of every wireless device you own.

events.label: Powered flight
events.blurb: Twelve seconds at Kitty Hawk. Sixty-six years later, people walked on the Moon.

events.label: Relativity
events.blurb: Einstein shows that space and time bend, and that gravity is geometry. Without the correction, GPS would drift kilometres off within a day.

events.label: The Tunguska airburst
events.blurb: An object explodes above Siberia and flattens 80 million trees across 2,000 square kilometres. Nobody is recorded as killed, and no crater was ever found.

events.label: The World Wars
events.blurb: Industrial-scale warfare kills perhaps 100 million people across two conflicts and reshapes the political map of the entire world.

events.label: The passenger pigeon goes extinct
events.blurb: Flocks once darkened the sky for days and numbered in the billions. Martha, the last one, died in a zoo in 1914. Abundance is no protection.

events.label: Quantum mechanics
events.blurb: Matter turns out to be probabilistic and granular at small scales. Strange as it is, it underpins every transistor, laser, and LED.

events.label: Penicillin
events.blurb: Fleming notices mould killing bacteria on a contaminated dish. Infections that routinely killed people become treatable.

events.label: The universe is expanding
events.blurb: Hubble finds that distant galaxies are all receding. The universe has a history and a beginning — which is how we know it is 13.8 billion years old.

events.label: The thylacine goes extinct
events.blurb: The last known Tasmanian tiger died in a Hobart zoo, two months after the species was finally granted legal protection.

events.label: Nuclear fission unleashed
events.blurb: Humans gain the ability to release the energy binding atoms together, and simultaneously the ability to end their own civilization.

events.label: The programmable computer
events.blurb: Machines that can be told what to do rather than rebuilt for each task. Turing had worked out what such a machine could do a decade earlier.

events.label: The transistor
events.blurb: A switch with no moving parts that can shrink almost indefinitely. There are now more transistors on Earth than grains of sand.

events.label: Universal Declaration of Human Rights
events.blurb: In the wake of the Second World War, 48 nations agree in writing that some rights belong to everyone simply for being human.

events.label: Human-driven change becomes global
events.blurb: CO2 climbs past any level in 3 million years, species are lost at hundreds of times the background rate, and human-made mass now outweighs all living biomass. Whether to formally name this the Anthropocene epoch is still contested.

events.label: The sixth mass extinction
events.blurb: Species are being lost at perhaps hundreds of times the natural background rate. Whether this yet qualifies as a true mass extinction is argued — the trend is not.

events.label: Structure of DNA solved
events.blurb: Watson, Crick, Franklin, and Wilkins reveal the double helix — the molecule that connects every organism on this timeline to every other.

events.label: The space age begins
events.blurb: A polished metal sphere beeping overhead every 96 minutes. Humanity has put something into orbit and kept it there.

events.label: The Keeling Curve begins
events.blurb: Charles Keeling starts measuring CO2 on Mauna Loa. The resulting sawtooth graph — the planet breathing, on a rising trend — becomes the defining chart of climate science.

events.label: The echo of the Big Bang is found
events.blurb: Two radio astronomers track a persistent hiss they assume is pigeon droppings. It turns out to be the afterglow of the universe's beginning.

events.label: Plate tectonics accepted
events.blurb: Fifty years after Wegener was mocked for it, seafloor evidence confirms continents move. Geology gets its unifying theory.

events.label: Humans walk on the Moon
events.blurb: About 66 million years after the asteroid, and 3.8 billion years after life began, a descendant of those first cells stands on another world.

events.label: Smallpox eradicated
events.blurb: A disease that killed perhaps 300 million people in the twentieth century alone is deliberately driven to extinction. It has never come back.

events.label: The ozone hole, found and fixed
events.blurb: A hole in the ozone layer is discovered over Antarctica. The world bans CFCs within two years, and it is now slowly closing — proof the thing can be done.

events.label: The Internet goes public
events.blurb: The World Wide Web is released to everyone. Within 30 years most of humanity is connected to it.

events.label: Planets found around other stars
events.blurb: The first confirmed exoplanets. Thousands are now known, and most stars appear to have planets.

events.label: Human genome sequenced
events.blurb: All 3 billion letters read. It confirms in detail what the fossils already suggested about our place on the tree of life.

events.label: The Higgs boson found
events.blurb: The particle explaining why matter has mass at all is detected, 48 years after it was predicted on paper.

events.label: CRISPR gene editing
events.blurb: A bacterial immune system is repurposed into precise, cheap genetic editing. For the first time we can rewrite the code this timeline is built from.

events.label: The Chelyabinsk meteor
events.blurb: A 20-metre rock explodes over Russia, injuring 1,500 people mostly through shattered glass. Nobody saw it coming — it arrived out of the Sun's glare.

events.label: Gravitational waves detected
events.blurb: Two black holes collide 1.3 billion light years away, and the ripple stretches a 4 km detector by less than the width of a proton.

events.label: mRNA vaccines
events.blurb: Vaccines designed in days rather than years, deployed to billions of people during a pandemic.

events.label: Eight billion humans
events.blurb: World population passes eight billion, with growth now slowing sharply as birth rates fall almost everywhere.

events.label: The James Webb Space Telescope
events.blurb: A telescope tuned to infrared light, seeing galaxies as they were within a few hundred million years of the Big Bang.
